what: The allocation column of std::profile, used to answer whether the d=256 gap to torch.compile is allocation or kernel: one thread, the same generated train_step.cml at d=256 and d=1024, the library-shape pipeline (tensor::fuse std::jit), 16 steps and 3 warm-up as in the earlier profiles.

machine.note: The host is shared; other builds and tests ran throughout. Absolute step times are therefore inflated and vary by a factor of two in this run. The allocation shares are ratios inside the same run and do not depend on the host's load.

method: Camel: std::profile report=true top=0 on the generated train_step.cml (measure.py's substitutions, run through a local generator with the same substitution list); operator rows are the 16-step run, the step block is the 15 measured rounds. A row's allocation column counts the time inside the Camel value allocators (block space payload, collected-heap object, permanent-space object) during that operator's calls, the allocator calls, the data blocks among them and the payload bytes of those blocks. A block's payload bytes are Block::create/grow's argument (the block space's rounded request, header and alignment are the allocator's own overhead). PyTorch was not re-run for this file: the question is the share inside Camel's own step, and the earlier paired profiles give the gap.

commands.profile_d256: camel -t 1 --block-limit 8192 train_step_256.cml tensor::fuse std::profile report=true 'json="prof-256.json"' top=0 std::jit --arg bench=true --arg init_dir= --arg final_dir=

allocations.counted: the block space (mm::Block::create/grow: tensor payloads and packing buffers), the collected heap (mm::autoSpace(): object headers, small arrays), the permanent space (mm::permSpace())
allocations.not_counted: a malloc behind new (a Block header, a std::vector buffer), a BLAS library's packing buffers, a memcpy over memory the kernel already owns, the page faults of first touching a newly reserved segment (charged to the kernel that writes the memory), and the free side (the report times allocations, not the free-list push or the collection that reclaims a block)
allocations.granularity: per operator URI, not per graph node; two nodes of one operator share a row, and a parallel operator's worker-thread allocations count as outside operator calls

categories.note: The category rows are the operator rows of the profile grouped; the full rows are below.

d256.note: tensor:sum_axis's allocation is a one-off block-space segment reservation, which lands on the call that first needs it; it is 4.06 ms of the 11.46 ms allocated inside operators, and it is not a per-step cost (the step row averages 0.68 ms).

overhead.enabled_cost: 5,976 operator calls and 26,771 allocator calls at 50 ns each is 1.64 ms over the 3.19 s d=256 run (0.05%); the allocation timer sits inside the operator's wall time, so the row is very slightly slower under the session
overhead.off_cost: one relaxed flag load and a not-taken branch per operator call, per allocation, and a handful of counter reads per loop round
overhead.observed: the program's own `naive bench` median was 164.09 ms with the pass and 144.27 ms without it (13.7%), but the same run's steps ranged 123.4-238.6 ms and the host carried load 60 on 32 threads; this difference is not separable from the host's noise, so only the arithmetic cost above is claimed

answer.question: Is the 34% d=256 gap to torch.compile allocator or kernel?
answer.answer: Kernel. At d=256 one step makes 362 block payloads (1,499 allocator calls, 137.9 MiB) and spends 0.68 ms inside the allocators, 0.40% of the step and 0.37% of the operator time; the three matmul rows spend 0.075% of their time in the allocator and allocate exactly one block per call, their output, so they also allocate no packing buffer. A 34% gap on the 66.1 ms step is about 22 ms, roughly 33 times the whole allocator work of a step. At d=1024 allocation is 1.34 ms of a 6.27 s step (0.02%) and 0.007% of the matmul rows.
answer.what_it_does_not_answer: The copies a kernel makes with memcpy, a BLAS library's own malloc'd packing buffers, the page faults of first touching a new segment, and the free/reclaim side (only allocations are timed) are still inside the kernel rows or not timed at all and cannot be split by this instrument; the answer rules out the Camel allocation calls, not every copy or the collector.

caveat_retired: The two earlier profiles had to write 'allocation and copying inside a kernel is not separable; std::profile times operator boundaries' and 'the matmul row includes its own packing and output allocation'. The allocation half is now measured (this file and docs/technical/54_profiler_allocations.md); the copying half is still not, and the report now says which of the two it can and cannot see instead of naming both as one unknown.
